slider.label: Mission duration (days)
notices: Approximation from separate crews. The line joins group averages from different missions (Space Shuttle and Mir, not ISS). Those crews also differed in exercise, so the line mixes mission length with other differences.

Straight-line approximation. This study measured this outcome once, after missions of one typical length. The line assumes change grows evenly from zero at launch to the measured value. No data in this study show that it does.
slider.supported: Supported range differs between the selected studies; it is listed under 'How the duration model works' for each.
sources: External source E1: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023)
statements: A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions, suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before ~4 mo of flight. — LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 3.
For example, the 17-day mission showed decreases up to ~10%, whereas the 4- to 6.5-mo missions showed maximum changes of only 17%. — LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 5.

view.summary: 9 published group results from Gopalakrishnan et al. (2010), LeBlanc et al. (2000), Scott et al. (2023); 9 measured at first postflight measurement of each study. Results are listed separately and are not combined.

title.text: Outcome against mission duration
Mission duration (days)
Change from the study's own baseline (%)

duration.caption: Filled markers are measured group values with their reported uncertainty; horizontal bars show the mission lengths behind them. Lines and open diamonds are model output (value type: approximation). Linear approximation: each straight line assumes change grows evenly from zero at launch to the single measured value. Dashed parts lie outside the mission lengths the study covers. Multi-cohort approximation: dotted parts join averages from separate Shuttle and Mir crews; the solid flat part is where LeBlanc et al. report no significant slope with duration. No ground-analogue (bed-rest) curve is drawn. The two bed-rest reviews in the external register are cited as context only.

models.title: LeBlanc et al. (2000) · Quadriceps muscle volume · Shuttle/Mir crew, American and Russian

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Group means from separate crews can be joined by straight segments, and the long-duration mean applies unchanged from 115 to 197 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: This is the only outcome with measured group means at more than one mission length. LeBlanc et al. report that percent loss had no significant slope against flight duration across 115–197 days, which supports a flat segment there. There are too few points to fit or test a curve, so no goodness-of-fit is given.

rows.text: 17–197 days (the shortest and longest flights with a measured group mean)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Repeated measurements of the same crew during flight, or group means from many mission lengths with the same exercise programme.

models.title: Scott et al. (2023) · Quadriceps cross-sectional area (MRI)

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 178 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 178 d: -5.74% (Scott et al. (2023), PDF page 3, Fig. 2 (printed table of estimates)); mission duration from PDF page 1: "Forty-six astronauts (37 males, 9 females; ... [mean ± SD]) were assigned to missions of 178 ± 48 d."

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 130–226 days (the reported mean ± one SD; this is not an observed minimum and maximum)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

rows.label: Notes and limitations
rows.text: Fig. 2 prints 'effect size (a, b)' for each endpoint and its caption calls the bracket a 95% CI. The effect size does not lie inside its bracket, and the bracket matches the percent changes given in the text for three endpoints (VO2peak −7.4% ± 2.0%; BMD −2.1% ± 0.7% and −3.7% ± 0.6%, PDF page 2), so the bracket is read here as the 95% CI of the mean percent change. The CI bounds are reported; the central value is an approximation (the CI midpoint, which assumes a symmetric interval) and agrees with the markers drawn in Fig. 1. To replace it: the per-endpoint means in Supplemental Tables 3–6, which are not in the local PDF.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

comparison.caption: Every study and cohort reporting this category and region at first postflight measurement of each study, each relative to its own baseline. Studies differ in population, method, timepoint and statistic, so the rows are shown together but never averaged. Bars are the uncertainty each source reports (SD, SE or 95% CI; see the tooltip).

models.title: Fitts et al. (2010) · Soleus type I fibre diameter · Low treadmill group

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 177 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 177 d: -25.96% (Fitts et al. (2010), PDF page 6, Table 2); mission duration from PDF page 2: "The subjects (n = 9) age, height, weight and days in space were 45 ± 2 years, 176 ± 2 cm, 81 ± 3 kg, and 177 ± 4 days (range = 161–192 days), respectively."

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 161–192 days (the reported minimum and maximum flight duration)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 177 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 161–192 days (the reported minimum and maximum flight duration)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

rows.label: Notes and limitations
rows.text: Fig. 2 prints 'effect size (a, b)' for each endpoint and its caption calls the bracket a 95% CI. The effect size does not lie inside its bracket, and the bracket matches the percent changes given in the text for three endpoints (VO2peak −7.4% ± 2.0%; BMD −2.1% ± 0.7% and −3.7% ± 0.6%, PDF page 2), so the bracket is read here as the 95% CI of the mean percent change. The CI bounds are reported; the central value is an approximation (the CI midpoint, which assumes a symmetric interval) and agrees with the markers drawn in Fig. 1. To replace it: the per-endpoint means in Supplemental Tables 3–6, which are not in the local PDF.

models.title: Trappe et al. (2009) · Calf maximal voluntary isometric contraction (neutral ankle angle)

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 177 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 177 d: -14% (Trappe et al. (2009), PDF page 5, Results text, 'Muscle performance'); mission duration from PDF page 2: "days in space were ... 177 ± 4 days (range = 161–192 days)"

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 161–192 days (the reported minimum and maximum flight duration)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

statements: A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions, suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before ~4 mo of flight. — LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 3.
For example, the 17-day mission showed decreases up to ~10%, whereas the 4- to 6.5-mo missions showed maximum changes of only 17%. — LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 5.

models.title: LeBlanc et al. (2000) · Anterior leg muscle volume · Shuttle/Mir crew, American and Russian

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Group means from separate crews can be joined by straight segments, and the long-duration mean applies unchanged from 115 to 197 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: This is the only outcome with measured group means at more than one mission length. LeBlanc et al. report that percent loss had no significant slope against flight duration across 115–197 days, which supports a flat segment there. There are too few points to fit or test a curve, so no goodness-of-fit is given.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

rows.text: Fig. 2 prints 'effect size (a, b)' for each endpoint and its caption calls the bracket a 95% CI. models.title: LeBlanc et al. (2000) · Intrinsic lower back muscle volume · Shuttle/Mir crew, American and Russian

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Group means from separate crews can be joined by straight segments, and the long-duration mean applies unchanged from 115 to 197 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: This is the only outcome with measured group means at more than one mission length. LeBlanc et al. report that percent loss had no significant slope against flight duration across 115–197 days, which supports a flat segment there. There are too few points to fit or test a curve, so no goodness-of-fit is given.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 8 d: -10.3% (External source E1, p. 27: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023)); 17 d: -10% (LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 4, Table 1); 161 d: -15.9% (LeBlanc et al. (2000), PDF page 3, Results text, 'Muscle volume')

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 8–197 days (the shortest and longest flights with a measured group mean)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Repeated measurements of the same crew during flight, or group means from many mission lengths with the same exercise programme.

rows.label: Sources
rows.text: LeBlanc et al. (2000) (Study Library); External source E1: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023)

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

models.title: Greene et al. (2021) · Trunk skeletal muscle cross-sectional area (CT, L2)

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 150 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 150 d: 0.8% (Greene et al. (2021), PDF page 17, Table 1); mission duration from PDF page 3: "15 males and 1 female who were on the ISS for 4–6 months"

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 120–180 days (an approximate range converted from the weeks or months the paper reports; no mean is reported, so the middle of the range is used as the reference)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

comparison.caption: Every study and cohort reporting this category and region at first postflight measurement of each study, each relative to its own baseline. Studies differ in population, method, timepoint and statistic, so the rows are shown together but never averaged. Bars are the uncertainty each source reports (SD, SE or 95% CI; see the tooltip).

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

models.title: English et al. (2020) · VO2peak (absolute) · SPRINT

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 152 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 152 d: 0.31% (English et al. (2020), PDF page 4, Table 4); mission duration from PDF page 6: "Mission duration (d)*: SPRINT 152 ± 24. *One subject completed a 340-d mission; that value is not included in the mission duration means"

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 128–176 days (the reported mean ± one SD; this is not an observed minimum and maximum)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

models.title: Scott et al. (2023) · Total body mass (DXA)

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 178 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

comparison.caption: Every study and cohort reporting this category and region at first postflight measurement of each study, each relative to its own baseline. Studies differ in population, method, timepoint and statistic, so the rows are shown together but never averaged. Bars are the uncertainty each source reports (SD, SE or 95% CI; see the tooltip).

models.title: Scott et al. (2023) · VO2peak

rows.label: Value type of every model output
What is assumed
rows.text: Change is zero at launch and grows in direct proportion to days in flight, reaching the measured value at 178 days.

rows.label: Why this model
rows.text: The study reports this outcome at a single postflight timepoint for one group of missions, so there is one data point. No published time-course function for this outcome in spaceflight was found, and one point cannot support a fitted curve.

rows.label: Anchored to
rows.text: 178 d: -7.4% (Scott et al. (2023), PDF page 2, Results text; 95% CI from Fig. 2 (PDF page 3)); mission duration from PDF page 1: "Forty-six astronauts (37 males, 9 females; ... [mean ± SD]) were assigned to missions of 178 ± 48 d."

rows.label: Supported range
rows.text: 130–226 days (the reported mean ± one SD; this is not an observed minimum and maximum)

rows.label: What would replace it
rows.text: Measurements of this outcome in flight or after missions of several different lengths under the same exercise programme.

context.label: E1 (spaceflight)
context.text: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023): 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.

context.label: E2 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures): Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

context.label: E3 (ground analogue, not spaceflight)
context.text: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only): Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

context.label: E4 (spaceflight)
context.text: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only): Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.

rows.text: On average, cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2peak) declined by 7.4% ± 2.0% from preflight to postflight (Fig. 1b). Fig. 2: VO2peak, Change pre-flight to R+1: -1.53 (-11.21, -3.55)

rows.label: Notes and limitations
rows.text: The mean is reported in the text as −7.4% ± 2.0% (the type of the ± value is not stated). The 95% CI is the bracket printed in Fig. 2 (PDF page 3), read as the CI of percent change for the reasons given on the other Scott records. Per-endpoint n is in Supplemental Table 2, which is not in the local PDF.

rows.label: Notes and limitations
rows.text: Fig. 2 prints 'effect size (a, b)' for each endpoint and its caption calls the bracket a 95% CI. The effect size does not lie inside its bracket, and the bracket matches the percent changes given in the text for three endpoints (VO2peak −7.4% ± 2.0%; BMD −2.1% ± 0.7% and −3.7% ± 0.6%, PDF page 2), so the bracket is read here as the 95% CI of the mean percent change. The CI bounds are reported; the central value is an approximation (the CI midpoint, which assumes a symmetric interval) and agrees with the markers drawn in Fig. 1. To replace it: the per-endpoint means in Supplemental Tables 3–6, which are not in the local PDF.
